note: For a 1 TB file the offset must be a 64-bit (8-byte) integer, because a 4-byte integer can only address about 4 GB.

note: In an LSM tree only the memtable (recent writes) is in memory; SSTables are sorted, immutable files on disk. Bitcask instead keeps every key (not values) in memory.
checker_note: In LSM designs the memtable holds the most recent writes (keys and values) in memory, but SSTables themselves are immutable on-disk files - values are not kept in memory overall. The accurate contrast: Bitcask keeps every key in RAM and values on disk; LSM keeps only recent writes in RAM and sorted keys and values on disk, so keys need not fit in memory.

additions.text: In Cassandra's write path every write goes first to the on-disk commit log, then to the in-memory memtable. Memtables are flushed to SSTables, which are immutable and never written again; with the default periodic commit-log sync (10 s) a crash can lose up to that window.

note: Bitcask appends every write straight to its data file, while an LSM engine appends to a write-ahead log and buffers in a memtable; in both, crash durability depends on how often the log is synced to disk.
checker_note: Two issues. (1) LSM engines do not lose memtable data on a crash by design: RocksDB and Cassandra write every update to a write-ahead/commit log before the memtable and replay it on restart (exposure depends only on the log sync setting). (2) Real Bitcask's default sync_strategy is 'none', which lets the OS decide when to flush; per-write durability needs o_sync. Both families trade durability against throughput through sync settings.

additions.text: Riak's Bitcask defaults to sync_strategy = none, which writes data into operating-system buffers and leaves flushing to the OS, so a power or OS failure before the flush can lose recent writes. Setting o_sync forces a sync on every write, at a throughput cost.
